subject: chemistry
title: Periodicity across Periods 2 and 3
key_idea: Properties repeat across each period because the outer electron configuration repeats. Atomic radius falls and first ionisation energy rises across a period. Melting point follows the structure: metallic, then giant covalent, then simple molecular.

blocks.text: The Periodic Table lists elements by increasing proton number. This section covers how position shows the outer electrons.

items.meaning: A repeating pattern in properties of the elements across each period.
A region of the table named after the sub-shell that holds the highest-energy outer electron: s, p, d or f.
A horizontal row. Elements in it fill the same outer shell.

items: **s-block**: Groups 1 and 2, where the outer electrons fill an s sub-shell.
**p-block**: Groups 13 to 18, where the outer electrons fill a p sub-shell.
**d-block**: the transition elements, where electrons fill a d sub-shell.
f-block: the lanthanoids and actinoids, set below the main table.

blocks.text: Electron configuration sets chemical properties. Elements in a group have the same outer configuration, so they react in similar ways.
Period 2 follows the same pattern with 2s and 2p. Lithium and beryllium are s-block. Boron to neon are p-block.

items: Block is set by where the highest-energy electron sits.
Periods repeat the same outer configurations, so properties repeat too.
Outer electrons decide whether an element loses, gains or shares electrons.

sections.heading: Atomic radius and first ionisation energy

blocks.text: Both quantities depend on the nuclear charge, the distance of the outer electron and the shielding by inner electrons. This section covers each trend across a period.

items: Atomic radius **decreases** across a period.
Each element has one more proton, so nuclear charge rises.
The extra electron goes into the same shell, so shielding hardly changes.
Outer electrons are pulled in more strongly.

blocks.label: First ionisation energy
where: X: one mole of gaseous atoms

items: It **increases** across a period overall, for the same reasons as the falling radius.
It falls sharply from the end of one period to the start of the next. The new outer electron is in a new shell: further out and better shielded.
Mg to Al falls. The 3p electron of Al is higher in energy than the 3s electrons of Mg and is shielded slightly by them.
P to S falls. In S the fourth 3p electron pairs with another in one orbital, and the repulsion makes it easier to remove.

blocks.text: Period 2 shows the same two dips, at Be to B and at N to O.

diagram.alt: Line graph of first ionisation energy against atomic number for sodium to argon. It rises overall, with small dips at aluminium and sulfur.

items: Atomic radius falls across a period as nuclear charge rises with no extra shell.
First ionisation energy rises overall, with dips at Group 13 and Group 16.
Both dips are explained by sub-shell energy and electron pairing.

blocks.text: Melting point depends on the structure and bonding, not on the atoms alone. This section covers Period 3, then the shape of the pattern.

rows: Attraction between cations and delocalised electrons

items: Na to Al: more delocalised electrons per atom and a smaller, more highly charged ion. The metallic bonding is stronger.
Si: a giant covalent lattice, so a very large amount of energy breaks the covalent bonds.
S₈ is higher than P₄, then Cl₂, then Ar. The larger the molecule, the more electrons and the stronger the London forces.
Boiling temperatures follow the same pattern as melting points.

blocks.text: Period 2 repeats the pattern. Lithium and beryllium are metallic. Boron and carbon are giant covalent with the highest melting points. N₂, O₂, F₂ and Ne are simple molecular and low.

items: Metals conduct because delocalised electrons move through the lattice. Conductivity rises from Na to Al as more electrons per atom are delocalised.
Silicon is a semiconductor: it conducts poorly.
P, S, Cl and Ar do not conduct. Their electrons are held in molecules or atoms and cannot move.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Put each Period 3 element into its structure type.
diagram.prompt: Sort each element by its structure.

items: Melting point rises Na to Al, peaks at Si, then drops for molecules.
Metals conduct because of delocalised electrons. Silicon is a semiconductor.
Always name the structure, then the bonds or forces that are overcome.

checks.q: Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.
checks.a: The outer electron removed from Al is in a 3p sub-shell, which is higher in energy than the 3s sub-shell of Mg. The 3p electron is also shielded slightly by the 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove.

checks.q: Explain why magnesium has a higher melting point than sodium.
checks.a: Both have giant metallic lattices. Mg has two delocalised electrons per atom and a smaller ion with a 2+ charge, so the attraction between ions and electrons is stronger. More energy is needed to overcome it.

checks.q: Explain why sulfur has a higher melting point than chlorine.
checks.a: Both are simple molecular, so London forces between molecules are overcome. S₈ is a larger molecule with more electrons than Cl₂, so its London forces are stronger and more energy is needed.

blocks.text: The Periodic Table has been refined as evidence grew. This part covers how the law of periodicity was developed and accepted.

items: Early tables were ordered by relative atomic mass. Elements were grouped by similar properties.
Mendeleev left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements. The elements later found, such as gallium and germanium, matched the predictions.
That success led the scientific community to accept the Periodic Law.
Ordering by proton number later fixed the pairs that had seemed out of order.
New elements are accepted once their discovery has been confirmed by other scientists, and the table is extended.

blocks.text: This part covers ionic radius and how to use periodicity to predict and deduce.

items: Na⁺, Mg²⁺ and Al³⁺ have the same 10 electrons. More protons pull them in, so the radius **decreases**: Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.
P³⁻, S²⁻ and Cl⁻ have 18 electrons. More protons again, so P³⁻ > S²⁻ > Cl⁻.
A cation is smaller than its atom because it has lost the outer shell.
An anion is larger than its atom because extra electrons repel each other.
Every anion in Period 3 is larger than every cation, because the anions have one more shell.
Position in a group tells you the outer configuration, so you can predict an element's usual ion, oxide formula and structure.
A large jump between successive ionisation energies shows the number of outer electrons, and so the group.
A high melting point with good conductivity suggests a metal. A very high melting point with poor conductivity suggests a giant covalent element.
Compare an unknown element's data with the known trend to place it in the table.
